title: Write the one-page spec
theme: Turn the decisions into a spec engineering can build and leadership can judge.
practised: Defining success metrics with baselines and targets
Revising a spec after engineering review
story_so_far: Week 1. Day 1: weak repeat comes from failed first orders (31% vs 6% repeat) and coupon customers. Day 2: focus first on morning commuters, who need reliable speed. Day 3: Café loses about ₹82 lakh a month; at 30% repeat it would make about ₹30 lakh a month. Day 4: Meera approved a two-week pilot called the 'First Order Promise': a Pune 3 km delivery cap; a 12-item 'Fast Lane' morning menu (7–11 am) in all 18 Pune kitchens and the 20 busiest Bengaluru kitchens; coupons only on first orders; extra morning staff; a targeted sorry credit when a first order goes wrong.
world_today: Today is Friday of week 1. Karthik's team needs a spec to plan next week's work.
canon_after_day: The First Order Promise spec v1 is approved: honest ETA with a +3-minute morning buffer; Fast Lane morning menu; Pune 3 km cap; coupons on first order only; a first-order quality check (sealed bag, checklist); and 'late or wrong first order, ₹50 back', with credits issued manually by support in v1 (automation later). The referral programme is deferred. Success metrics: first-order on-time from 64% to 85%; first-order complaints from 9% to under 4%; 7-day repeat of first-time customers from 9% to 14%; margin per order; credit cost. Karthik initially estimates the full spec at 5 weeks.

inbox.subject: Spec day
inbox.body:
Great work yesterday. Now write the First Order Promise as a one-page spec Karthik can plan from and leadership can judge.

Keep it to one page: problem, who it's for, what we'll build (and won't), how we'll measure success, risks. Get baselines from Lakshmi and constraints from Karthik before you write. Send it to me, then Karthik will review it.

Meera

documents.title: One-page spec template
documents.body: Problem and evidence · Who it's for · What we'll build (v1) · Out of scope · Success metrics (baseline → target) · Risks and mitigations · Dependencies · Open questions

characters.opener: Spec day. One page. Baselines and targets on every metric, please.
characters.today: If asked, remind the player that a good spec says what is out of scope. Don't write it for them.

characters.opener: Hi! Need baselines for your spec? Precise questions, up to 25 pulls.

hidden_facts.fact: First-order on-time rate (arrived within the promised ETA): 64% overall; Bengaluru 68%, Pune 52%.
hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked for the on-time rate of first orders

hidden_facts.reveal_if: Asked for the complaint rate on first orders

message.text: Small ask 🙏 Can we add a referral feature to the spec? 'Give ₹100, get ₹100.' It's tiny and it brings new customers in for the Promise!
Thanks, reading it now. Sending it to Karthik for review too.

ai_reply.direction: Review the spec honestly in 3–4 lines. Estimate the full spec as written at about 5 weeks. Flag the two biggest issues among: automatic credits need the payments team (3 weeks), the ETA promise is not honest without the morning buffer, anything vague. Ask what can move to later.

scoring.strong_player: Gets baselines (on-time 64%, complaints 9%, 7-day repeat 9%) and constraints (ETA 4 minutes too optimistic, auto-credits need 3 weeks) before writing; writes a genuine one-pager with metrics as baseline → target; names out of scope; turns down the referral feature for v1 with a reason (it brings in new customers before the first order is fixed, and referred-style incentives attract one-timers); responds to Karthik by moving automatic credits and the model fix to later, using manual credits and a fixed morning buffer.

expected_answers.t1: Ask Lakshmi for first-order on-time, complaint and 7-day repeat baselines by city, and the cost of the credit. Ask Karthik how honest the ETA is in the morning, how the credit would be built, and the effort of each part.
expected_answers.t2: Problem: first orders fail (64% on time, 9% complaints) and failed first orders repeat at 6% vs 31%. For: first-time customers, especially weekday morning commuters. v1: honest ETA (+3 min morning buffer), Fast Lane menu, Pune 3 km cap, coupons on first order only, first-order quality check, '₹50 back if late or wrong' issued by support. Out of scope: shared cart, referral programme, automatic credits, ETA model rebuild. Metrics: on-time 64% → 85%, complaints 9% → under 4%, 7-day repeat 9% → 14%, margin per order, credit cost (about ₹2.5–6 lakh a week). Risks: credit abuse (one per customer), lost Pune orders, kitchen staffing gaps.
expected_answers.t3: Not in v1. A referral programme brings more people to a first order we haven't fixed yet, and incentive-driven customers repeat poorly (coupon customers repeat at 8%). Offer to revisit once on-time is above 85% for two weeks.
expected_answers.t4: Agree with Karthik to cut to what ships in about a week: config changes (radius, menu, coupon rule, +3 min morning buffer), kitchen checklist (no tech), manual credits by support. Move the badge, automatic credits and ETA model fix to phase 2. Confirm the revised estimate and the start date.

common_mistakes: Saying yes to the referral feature
Defending the spec instead of cutting scope with Karthik
scoring.senior_view: A senior PM would collect baselines first, write a tight one-pager where every metric has a number and a target, and make out of scope explicit. They'd say 'not now, here's when' to the referral ask, and treat Karthik's review as a chance to find the smallest version that tests the idea.
scoring.drill: Take any feature you know. Write its success metrics as 'metric: baseline → target by date' for three metrics, plus one guardrail metric that must not get worse.
